section.title: The Birth of Jesus
section.sectionRationale: The promises of the songs now take flesh. A decree from Caesar sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, the city of David, where the Savior is born and laid in a manger. The first to hear the news are not emperors or priests but shepherds keeping watch by night, to whom an angel announces good news of great joy: a Savior, Christ the Lord. The heavenly host praise God, the shepherds run to see, and Mary treasures it all. It is one movement, from the machinery of empire to a manger, and from a manger to the songs of heaven.
section.thesis: While Caesar counts his empire, God quietly keeps His promise: the Savior, Christ the Lord, is born in David's town and laid in a manger, and heaven's glory breaks over lowly shepherds with good news of great joy and peace for all the people.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the census and the journey to Bethlehem; the birth in a manger; the angel's good news to the shepherds; the shepherds' visit and Mary's treasured heart; and the naming of Jesus.

units.label: The census and the journey to Bethlehem

verses.text: Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire.
This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
And everyone went to his own town to register.
So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David.
He went there to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child.

units.label: The birth in a manger
units.note: no room for them in the inn

verses.text: While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born.
And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a {{phatne|manger}}, because there was no room for them in the inn.

units.label: The angel's good news to the shepherds

verses.text: And there were shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night.
Just then an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great {{chara|joy}} that will be for all the people:
Today in the city of David a {{soter|Savior}} has been born to you. He is {{christos|Christ}} the Lord!
And this will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”
And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying:
“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth {{eirene|peace}} to men on whom His favor rests!”

units.label: The shepherds visit, and Mary treasures it all
units.note: they spread the message about Him

verses.text: When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger.
After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him.
And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them.
But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.

units.label: The naming of Jesus
units.note: the name the angel had given

verses.text: When the eight days before His circumcision had passed, He was named Jesus, the name the angel had given Him before He was conceived.

phatne.gloss: A manger, a feeding trough for animals. The Lord of glory is laid where beasts feed, a sign of the humility of His coming and of a Savior who makes Himself known to the lowly. The manger is even the sign the angel gives the shepherds.

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness. The angel brings good news of great joy for all the people. Joy rings through Luke's Gospel, and here it is offered not to a privileged few but to everyone, beginning with shepherds in a field.

soter.gloss: Savior, deliverer. The child is announced as a Savior born for you. In a world that hailed Caesar as savior and lord, the angel gives both titles to a baby in a manger, the true Rescuer of His people.

christos.gloss: Christ, the Anointed One, the Messiah, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Mashiach. The angel declares the child to be Christ the Lord, the long-awaited King from David's line, now born in David's town.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, the fullness of the Hebrew shalom. The heavenly host announce peace on earth to those on whom God's favor rests, the reconciliation with God that the Savior comes to bring.

basic.context: A census ordered by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, because Joseph belongs to David's line. There Jesus is born and laid in a manger, since there was no room in the inn. Nearby, shepherds are keeping watch at night when an angel appears in blazing glory and announces good news of great joy: a Savior, Christ the Lord, has been born, and the sign is a baby in a manger. A host of angels praises God. The shepherds hurry to see, then spread the news, while Mary quietly treasures it all. On the eighth day the child is named Jesus.
basic.hermeneutics: Luke sets the birth against the backdrop of the world's greatest power, Caesar, only to show that the real King enters in weakness. The shepherds, humble and even ceremonially suspect, are the first evangelists, which fits Luke's theme of a Savior for the lowly. The angelic titles Savior, Christ, and Lord are deliberately loaded, given elsewhere to Caesar. The key questions are who this baby is and why God announces Him first to the poor.
basic.originalLanguages: The Savior is laid in a phatne, a manger, the sign of His humble coming. The angel brings good news of great chara, joy, for all people: a soter, a Savior, who is christos, Christ, the Lord. The heavenly host announce eirene, peace, on earth to those on whom God's favor rests.
basic.typology: Bethlehem, the city of David, fulfills Micah's prophecy of the ruler to come from that little town. The manger and the shepherds echo David the shepherd-king. The peace announced by the angels is the true peace long promised, greater than any Roman peace enforced by the sword.
basic.christ: This is the incarnation itself: the eternal Son born as a human baby. He is named Savior, Christ, and Lord in a single breath, the whole gospel in a sentence, and He is born for you, for all the people.
basic.god: God rules over emperors, bending even Caesar's decree to place the Savior's birth in David's town. He reveals His glory to shepherds, gives peace to the undeserving, and keeps every promise. His grace runs to the lowly.
basic.crossReferences: Micah 5 foretells the ruler born in Bethlehem. Isaiah 9 promises the Prince of Peace. Titus 2 speaks of the grace of God that brings salvation appearing to all. And Philippians 2 describes the Son who emptied Himself and took the form of a servant.
basic.oneStory: The Savior promised through the ages is finally born, and heaven cannot keep silent. The King enters His world in a manger, announced first to shepherds, offered to all the people. The good news of great joy has come, and the peace of God is breaking over the earth.

context.literary:
Luke 2:1-21 is built as a story told on two stages at once. The first stage is the world's: a decree, an emperor, a governor, an empire-wide registration. The second is a stable and a hillside. Luke moves between them with remarkable economy, giving the great stage two verses and a half, and the small one the rest. The opening, 'Now in those days,' is the idiom of biblical narrative and not of Roman history writing, a signal that this is the next chapter of the story begun in Israel's Scriptures.

The passage has a three-part movement. Verses 1 to 7 are the birth, told with almost no adjectives. Verses 8 to 20 are the longest unit, the revelation to the shepherds, which itself has a rise and a fall: an angel appears and the glory shines, verse 9; the message is given, verses 10 to 12; the army of heaven sings, verses 13 and 14; the shepherds go, find, tell and return, verses 15 to 20. Verse 21 then closes the scene with the circumcision and the naming, which brings the story back to the law and to Gabriel's original word.

The manger is the thread that holds the structure together. It is mentioned in verse 7 as the place the child is laid, in verse 12 as the sign the shepherds will look for, and in verse 16 as the place where they find Him. A phrase repeated three times in seven verses is Luke's way of underlining it. The angel's sign is not a blazing star but the plainest thing imaginable, a baby wrapped and lying in a feeding trough. The great fear of verse 9 is matched by the 'great joy' of verse 10, a deliberate pair, and the shepherds who 'glorify and praise' in verse 20 take up the very word used of the angels in verse 13.

The passage also sits in a larger Lukan pattern of reversals. The Magnificat has just sung that God has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the lowly, Luke 1:52. Here, at the first opportunity, the pattern is shown rather than sung.
context.historical:
Luke fixes the story in Roman history. Augustus, who ruled from 27 BC to AD 14, was celebrated in the empire as a bringer of peace after decades of civil war, and the emperor's birthday and accession were marked as good news. An inscription from Priene in Asia Minor praises his birth as the beginning of 'glad tidings' for the world and calls him savior. A first hearer in the Greek-speaking empire would have recognized the vocabulary the angel borrows, and would have recognized that it is being taken from Caesar and given to a child in a feeding trough.

The census is one of the most discussed details in the passage. Roman provincial registrations were used for taxation and sometimes for enrolling people in their places of origin; a later papyrus edict from Egypt orders those living away from home to return to their own districts for the census. Joseph's journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem, about ninety miles by the roads he would have used, is therefore not strange in kind. The difficulty is the date. Luke says this was the first census while Quirinius was governor of Syria, and the historian Josephus records a census in Judea under Quirinius in AD 6, an event that provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean that Luke himself mentions in Acts 5:37. Since Luke also places the birth in the days of Herod the Great, Luke 1:5, who died around 4 BC, the relation between the two dates has been argued for centuries.

Bethlehem lay on the ridge about five or six miles south of Jerusalem, a small town in Judah known as Ephrathah. It was the town of Ruth and Boaz, Ruth 4:11, and the home of Jesse, where Samuel found the youngest son tending sheep, 1 Samuel 16:11 to 13. The flocks of the region were grazed in the fields outside the town. Genesis 35:21 mentions a Tower of Eder near the road to Bethlehem, and Micah 4:8 calls Zion the watchtower of the flock, so a tradition of pasture and of shepherding was woven into the landscape.

Houses in a town like Bethlehem were typically of one main room, with a lower section where animals might be brought in at night. Mary's wrapping of the baby in strips of cloth was the ordinary care of any newborn.
context.canonical:
Luke's birth account is thick with the Old Testament, though he quotes less than Matthew does. The place is the first anchor. Micah named Bethlehem Ephrathah as the town from which a ruler of Israel would come, Micah 5:2, and added that the ruler would shepherd the flock in the strength of the LORD and be Israel's peace, Micah 5:4 and 5. Matthew quotes it directly at Matthew 2:5 and 6. Luke does not, but his two uses of 'the city of David,' in verses 4 and 11, plus the shepherds, say the same thing in narrative form. David was brought from the sheepfold to shepherd God's people, Psalm 78:70 to 72, and the prophets promised another shepherd-king of David's line, Ezekiel 34:23.

The angel's words recall Isaiah. 'A child is born' and 'good news' bring to mind Isaiah 9:6 and Isaiah 52:7, and the shepherds' reaction fits the passage in which the glory of the LORD is revealed to all flesh, Isaiah 40:5. The 'host' is the 'host of heaven' of the Old Testament, the angelic armies that serve God, Psalm 103:20 and 21 and Psalm 148:2.

The New Testament picks up Luke's themes in other keys. Paul says that when the fullness of time had come God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, Galatians 4:4, and that though rich He became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9. Philippians 2 describes the same descent as a self-emptying, Philippians 2:7. Hebrews says that when God brings His firstborn into the world He commands all angels to worship Him, Hebrews 1:6, so what the angels do here is the application of that command.

The angels' song returns at the end of Luke's Gospel, when the crowds on the Mount of Olives say 'Peace in heaven and glory in the highest,' Luke 19:38, so the Gospel of Luke opens and closes with the same hymn at different edges of Jesus' life. The 'sign' of verse 12 echoes Isaiah 7:14, where the sign is also a child.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his reader to be certain of what he has been taught, Luke 1:4, and for that purpose he places the birth in the daylight of recorded history. The decree, the governor and the town are facts that anyone in the empire could in principle check. Yet he does not tell the story for the sake of chronology. His real aim is to show who the child is and what He is for. The great powers of the world move across the stage only to bring a couple to the right town at the right time, and the angel announces that the person who matters is not on any imperial list.

He also intends to show the pattern of God's grace. The first people to be told are working people at night, and they are not given a title or a lesson, only a sign and a Savior. Luke will tell the same story again and again: the poor have the gospel preached to them, Luke 7:22; the lost are sought, Luke 19:10. The shepherds are an early instance, and the reader is meant to see that the gospel is for such people.

Luke finally wants readers to join the response. The shepherds hurry, look, speak and praise, and Mary stores it up and thinks it over. Between them they set out two ways to receive good news, one in outward testimony and one in quiet reflection. Luke, who is writing to someone who has been taught about Jesus, offers both as a model.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Luke records a night in the countryside and an angelic song; he does not set out a rule for how the birth of Christ must be observed. Nothing in the passage prescribes a date, a calendar or a form of celebration, and Scripture nowhere says to mark the occasion. Whatever Christians do with Christmas must be argued from wisdom and gratitude and not from this text. What the passage does give is the content of what is worth celebrating, a Savior who is Christ the Lord.

It is also a description, not a command, that the baby was laid in a manger because there was no room. The detail tells us about the Son's humility. It does not teach that poverty is a sign of God's favor, or that the shepherds' social standing made them better recipients than others. Luke includes wealthy and powerful people elsewhere in his Gospel who also come to faith, Luke 19:9.

The verbs the shepherds use are worth carrying forward. They hear, they go, they see, they tell, they glorify. Those are not obligations imposed by the text, but they are a fair model of the way a person responds to good news that is true. A reader who has also been told the news of great joy for all the people is invited to treat it the same way, as news to be verified in Christ and then shared.

debates.question: What do the dates of Luke's census and Quirinius mean?

views.label: Luke is speaking of an earlier registration
views.case: Luke 2:2 can be read as 'This registration took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria,' since the Greek word for 'first' can take a genitive and mean 'before,' as it does in John 1:15, where John says Jesus was 'before me.' On this reading Luke separates this census from the better known one of AD 6, which he mentions himself at Acts 5:37.

views.label: Quirinius held an earlier command
views.case: Some propose that Quirinius had a special military or administrative role in the region earlier than his formal governorship, so that Luke is naming the man by his later famous title. Others suggest that registrations in client kingdoms such as Herod's could have happened on Rome's order, with the dating at the end of Herod's reign.

views.label: Luke has compressed or misdated events
views.case: A number of historians conclude that Luke has run two events together, taking the well known census of AD 6 and applying it to the birth. They note that the extant sources do not describe an empire-wide census in Herod's last years.

debates.bearing: The data is not complete and honest readers differ. What does not change is the theological point: the birth of Jesus was in real time and place, and it was God, not Caesar, who ordered the journey. A reader can hold the question of the exact census open without loosening the claim that Jesus was born in Bethlehem of David's line, which Matthew and Luke each affirm independently.

debates.question: Was the baby born in a stable or in a family home?

views.label: A crowded inn, with the child laid among animals
views.case: The traditional picture takes the word translated 'inn' as a public lodging and places the birth in a stable or cave nearby. The manger shows that animals were present, and the tradition is old.

views.label: A family home with a full guest room
views.case: The Greek word is kataluma, which Luke uses again for the 'guest room' where Jesus eats the Passover in Luke 22:11. When Luke wants a commercial inn he uses a different word, in Luke 10:34. A town like Bethlehem would offer hospitality through relatives, and the guest room may have been full, so the birth took place in the main room where the animals' feeding trough stood.

debates.bearing: The second reading fits Luke's own vocabulary and Joseph's family ties to Bethlehem, but it changes little. Either way the Son of God was born in crowded, borrowed space, and Luke's message of humility holds.

debates.question: Who receives the peace of verse 14?

views.label: Those on whom God's favor rests
views.case: The better attested Greek text has 'men of good pleasure,' a genitive that points to people God has favored, which the BSB renders 'men on whom His favor rests.' This puts the weight on God's grace as the source of peace.

views.label: Peace and goodwill to all
views.case: The older reading, from which the King James translation came, has the nominative, 'goodwill toward men,' which makes the angels announce a general disposition of God toward humanity. It echoes the angel's 'for all the people' in verse 10.

debates.bearing: The two readings are less far apart than they look. God's goodwill is for all, as the angel says, and the peace is given to those who receive the child. The Gospel keeps both truths: the offer is universal, as Luke 2:10 says, and the enjoyment of peace is for those who welcome Him, as Luke 10:5 and 6 and Luke 19:42 also suggest.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 7 says the child was laid in a manger because there was no room 'in the inn,' and the word behind it, kataluma, is worth a second look. It is built on a verb meaning to loosen or unharness, so it names a place where travellers set down their loads. Luke uses it again of the room where Jesus will eat His last Passover, Luke 22:11, where it is the 'guest room' of a house. When Luke wants a commercial lodging, as in the story of the Samaritan, he uses a different word, pandocheion, Luke 10:34. That shifts the likely picture from a roadside hostel to a crowded family house.

The angel's announcement uses the verb euangelizomai, 'I bring you good news,' in verse 10. It is the verb Isaiah uses for the messenger who declares that God reigns, Isaiah 52:7, and Luke uses it of Jesus' own mission in Luke 4:18 and 4:43. The cognate noun was also the word used in the Greek world for the announcement of an emperor's accession or birthday. Luke chooses it knowingly. The real good news is not a decree from a palace but a birth in a town.

Verse 11 begins with semeron, 'today,' which is a favorite word in Luke. It marks the moment when God's promise becomes present: 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled,' Luke 4:21, 'Today salvation has come to this house,' Luke 19:9, and 'Today you will be with Me in paradise,' Luke 23:43. The angel's 'today' is the first of these, announcing that the time of waiting has ended.

Verse 9 says the shepherds feared 'a great fear,' using a cognate construction, ephobethesan phobon megan, and verse 10 answers with 'great joy.' The doubling of the two 'greats' is a literary signal. The angel's first command, 'Do not be afraid,' turns the dread of encountering glory into the gladness of receiving a gift.

Verse 13 calls the angelic company a stratia ouranios, a 'heavenly host,' and stratia is the word for an army. In the Old Testament God is the LORD of Hosts, the commander of heaven's armies. The army of heaven appears not to fight but to sing, and the first words of its song are 'Glory to God in the highest.' In Luke 2:14 the last clause is anthropois eudokias, a phrase in which eudokia, 'good pleasure,' is in the genitive, which is why the BSB reads 'men on whom His favor rests.'

Verse 15 has the shepherds say they will see 'this thing,' using rhema, a word that means both 'word' and 'event.' The Hebrew counterpart, davar, has the same double sense. What God has said has happened. In verse 19 Mary 'treasured' these rhemata and 'pondered' them, using symballo, whose basic sense is to throw together, to put side by side. She is laying events and words next to each other to see how they fit, which is what readers of the Gospel are being asked to do.

typology.fulfillment: The town where David was found among the sheep and anointed, 1 Samuel 16:11 to 13, is the town where David's greater descendant is born. Micah had called it small among the clans of Judah and promised that out of it would come a ruler whose origins are from the days of eternity, Micah 5:2. The correspondence is of place and line, and it deepens in Christ because He is not merely a son of David but David's Lord, Luke 20:41 to 44. The type falls short in that David ruled one nation for forty years, while the Child born here reigns over all the nations, and His kingdom has no end, Luke 1:33.

The promise of a shepherd-king runs through the Old Testament. David was taken from the sheep to shepherd Israel, 2 Samuel 5:2, and God Himself said He would search for His scattered flock and appoint over it one shepherd, His servant David, Ezekiel 34:11 to 23. Shepherds are the first to be told that this shepherd has arrived. Jesus later says, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and that He lays down His life for the sheep. The pattern is exact in its theme and surprising in its cost. The point at which the type falls short is that David's care did not extend to dying for his flock, and Christ's does.

typology.type: The firstborn laid in a feeding trough
typology.fulfillment: Luke calls the child Mary's 'firstborn,' and Israel's firstborn belonged to the LORD, Exodus 13:2. Jesus is the true firstborn, 'the firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15, and when God brings His firstborn into the world the angels are told to worship Him, Hebrews 1:6. The correspondence is between a consecrated son and the Son who is consecrated for all. The escalation is that He lies in the animals' trough while the angels adore. Paul's phrase, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, interprets it. The type falls short in that the firstborn of Israel were redeemed by a price, while this Firstborn is the price.

When King Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, God gave one anyway, a child whose name is Immanuel, Isaiah 7:14, and Isaiah promised a child on whose shoulders government would rest, Isaiah 9:6. The angel's 'sign' of verse 12 is also a baby. The correspondence runs on the theme that God's deliverance of His people takes the form of a child. In Jesus the sign is fulfilled in the strongest way, since 'God with us' is not a name but a fact, Matthew 1:23. A sign points beyond itself, and the type falls short in that this sign is also the thing signified.

study.christ:
The passage does not stop at declaring that a child was born. It names Him in three titles in a single sentence of the angel, and each title carries a distinct strand of Old Testament hope. 'Savior' recalls that the LORD alone is the Savior of Israel, Isaiah 43:11, and Mary has already sung 'God my Savior,' Luke 1:47. 'Christ' is the anointed king of David's line, the one promised in 2 Samuel 7:12 and 13. 'Lord' is the title the Greek Old Testament gives to the LORD Himself. Taken together, they say that the one lying in the manger is God's answer to Israel's longing and also a person who shares God's own name. Peter will say much the same on Pentecost, that God has made Him both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36, and Acts 10:36 adds that He is Lord of all.

The incarnation is the very heart of the passage. John states it as the Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us, John 1:14, and Paul calls it the mystery of godliness, that He appeared in the flesh, 1 Timothy 3:16. Hebrews explains why: since the children share flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14. The manger is therefore not only a picture of humility. It is the first stage of a rescue that will end at a cross. The child who is wrapped in cloths is the One who will later be wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb, Luke 23:53.

The passage also shows His rule in contrast to Caesar's. Augustus was proclaimed lord and savior and was thought to have brought peace, but the peace of the empire was won by armies. The peace of this child is the peace that Micah promised when he said that the ruler of Bethlehem would be Israel's peace, Micah 5:5, and that Paul describes when he says Christ Himself is our peace, who has reconciled both Jew and Gentile to God through the cross, Ephesians 2:14 to 16. The peace that the angels announce is not the end of war between nations but the end of enmity between people and God.

He is born 'for you,' and 'for all the people.' The message is both particular and universal, and Luke will carry the point forward in Simeon's words about a light for the Gentiles in Luke 2:32. Whoever hears is told that the Savior has been born to them.

A word of caution applies. Not every detail of the account is a hidden picture of Christ. The inn, the animals and the stars of later Christmas imagination are not coded messages. The links that matter are those the New Testament makes itself: He is the descendant of David, the firstborn, the Son who is made like His brothers in every way, Hebrews 2:17, and the Savior whom no other name can replace, Acts 4:12.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is the Lord of history. The empire's most powerful man issues a decree for his own purposes, and the effect is that a poor couple is moved to a small town exactly where a prophet had said a ruler would be born. Scripture holds that God changes times and seasons and removes and sets up kings, Daniel 2:21, and that the king's heart is like channels of water in the LORD's hand, Proverbs 21:1. Luke gives that conviction a concrete example. Caesar believes he is counting subjects, and he is in fact fulfilling a promise.

God is also the God who stoops. The psalmist asks who is like the LORD our God, who sits enthroned on high and yet humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth, and who raises the poor from the dust, Psalm 113:5 to 8. Isaiah says that the high and holy One dwells with the oppressed and humble in spirit, Isaiah 57:15. The birth narrative takes this from poetry and puts it in a feeding trough. The doctrine of God that comes from this is that majesty and condescension are not opposites in Him. He does not become less God by becoming small, and His glory is most clearly displayed in His willingness to be where the lowly are.

He is a God of glory who also reassures. The glory of the Lord shines around the shepherds, and the first thing the angel says is that they should not be afraid. The holiness of God does not mean that He wants to terrify people but that, when His presence comes near, He first speaks peace. That is a quiet but important correction to any picture of God as a distant or hostile judge.

He is a God who gives joy. The word 'joy' is part of the announcement from the beginning, and the shepherds return glorifying and praising God. A believer's worship is meant to be glad, because the news is good.

He is faithful to what He has said. The shepherds find everything 'just as the angel had told them,' verse 20. The name given to the child is 'the name the angel had given Him before He had been conceived,' verse 21. What God says comes to pass, down to a name and a trough.

A Trinitarian shape lies under the surface of the story. The Father sends the Son, the angel of the Lord speaks and the host sings. Luke's earlier chapters have the Spirit and the power of the Most High overshadowing Mary, Luke 1:35, so that the birth in verse 7 is the work of the whole Godhead.

For worship, the passage teaches two postures at once. The shepherds go in haste to see for themselves, which is the posture of faith that seeks, and they leave glorifying God, which is the posture of faith that has found. A worshiper is both a seeker and a witness.

crossReferences.note: Micah names Bethlehem Ephrathah as the town from which Israel's ruler comes, says His origins are from days of eternity, and promises that He will stand and shepherd in the LORD's strength and be Israel's peace. Luke's 'city of David' and the angel's peace are the fulfillment, and Matthew quotes the same passage at Matthew 2:5 and 6.

Samuel finds the youngest son of Jesse tending sheep, and God says 'Rise and anoint him.' The shepherd boy of Bethlehem becomes king. The same town, the same occupation and the same unlikeliness appear on the night of Luke 2, where shepherds are the first to hear that David's heir has been born.

A child is born, a son is given, and His government and peace will have no end. He will reign on David's throne. The angel's good news of a child with a throne and with peace is the New Testament voice of this passage, and Gabriel has already used its throne language at Luke 1:32 and 33.

The feet of the messenger who proclaims peace and good news and says 'Your God reigns' are beautiful, and all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of God. The angel's good news of great joy for all the people is the fulfillment, and its verb is the one Luke uses in verse 10.

Mary sings that God has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the humble, and has filled the hungry. Chapter 2 acts it out. The ruler of the world is moved by his own decree, while the lowly receive heaven's first announcement. The Magnificat gives the pattern and the birth narrative shows it.

At the descent from the Mount of Olives the disciples praise God for His miracles and cry out 'Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.' It is the angels' song of Luke 2:14 taken up by people. Luke begins and ends Jesus' public coming with this hymn, tying the baby to the king who enters Jerusalem.

When the time had fully come God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law. Paul's summary explains the point of the birth in Luke. The Son's entry into the human condition, including circumcision on the eighth day in verse 21, is for our adoption.

Christ, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. The self-emptying describes in theological terms what Luke narrates in a manger. Paul adds that the humility led to death on a cross, which shows where the manger leads.

The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone, and He gave Himself to redeem and purify a people for His own possession. The words 'appeared' and 'salvation to everyone' reflect the angel's 'for all the people.' Paul even calls Jesus 'our great God and Savior' in verse 13.

When God brings His firstborn into the world, He says 'Let all God's angels worship Him.' This is the theology behind the heavenly host of Luke 2:13. The angels are not only messengers to the shepherds; they are worshipers of the child, because the child is the Son.

God says He Himself will search for His scattered flock, seek the lost and bring back the strays. Shepherds are therefore the apt first audience for a birth that begins God's own shepherding. Jesus applies the image to Himself in John 10:11 and 14, and in Luke 19:10 He says He came to seek and save the lost.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creation that God called very good and with human beings who were made to rule under Him. Genesis 3 records the rupture and the promise of an offspring who would crush the serpent's head. Everything between that promise and Luke 2 is the story of how God kept it alive: the line of Seth and Noah, the call of Abraham, the covenant with David, the prophets who spoke of a child, a shepherd and a king, and the exile that seemed to cut the line off. Luke 2 is the moment the promise takes a body.

It answers what had come before in several ways. To a people who had asked for centuries whether God was still faithful, it answers with a name, a place and a date. To the prophets who had spoken of a Bethlehem ruler, a child on David's throne, a light for the nations and a peace without end, it gives a face. To the question of Genesis 3 about whether God would deal with the damage done to the human race, it gives a Son who is born of a woman, Galatians 4:4, and who will share flesh and blood to undo what the enemy did, Hebrews 2:14.

It also sets up everything that follows. The naming in verse 21 leads straight to the temple in the next scene, where Simeon says he has seen salvation. The manger anticipates the cross, since the one who is wrapped in cloths and laid in a place not made for Him is the one who will later be laid in a tomb no one else has used, Luke 23:53. The shepherds' testimony anticipates the apostolic witness, and Mary's pondering anticipates the way the church would hold these events in the heart. The song of the angels returns in Luke 19:38 when the King comes to Jerusalem.

In the larger story, the birth is the hinge between promise and fulfillment. God has spoken to the fathers by the prophets, and in these last days He has spoken by His Son, Hebrews 1:1 and 2. The kingdom of the child is one that will draw people from every nation, and the vision of Revelation sees myriads of angels with the nations around the throne, saying 'Worthy is the Lamb,' Revelation 5:11 to 13. The song that began over Bethlehem fields is finished there, and the child of the feeding trough is revealed as the Lamb on the throne.

The new creation is the end of this chapter, as of every chapter. In it, 'the dwelling of God is with men,' Revelation 21:3, and the Son who once had no room in a house has made room for everyone who comes to Him, John 14:2. The peace announced over the shepherds is received in full.

sermon.title: A Savior, Christ the Lord
sermon.why: Begg expounds Luke 2:8-12, showing how God used an angelic announcement to lowly shepherds to declare that He has provided salvation in Christ alone for all people, good news of great joy. A faithful, expository handling of the birth announcement at the center of this movement.

quiz.q: Why did Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem?

options.text: A census ordered by Caesar required registration, and Joseph belonged to the house of David, whose town was Bethlehem.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 give the census and Joseph's Davidic descent as the reason.

options.text: Because Bethlehem was where Joseph's family lived.
options.note: True that he was of David's line and town, but the immediate cause was the census requiring registration.

options.text: Because an angel told them to go there to give birth.
options.note: No angel directed the journey; a Roman decree brought them, under God's providence.

options.text: Because Nazareth had been destroyed.
options.note: Nothing happened to Nazareth; they went for the census.

quiz.q: To whom did the angel first announce the Savior's birth?

options.text: To shepherds keeping watch over their flocks by night.
options.note: Verses 8 to 11 show the news came first to lowly shepherds.

options.text: To ordinary working people rather than the powerful.
options.note: True in substance, but the text names shepherds specifically.

options.text: To the priests in the temple at Jerusalem.
options.note: The priests were not told; the shepherds were.

options.text: To Caesar Augustus and his officials.
options.note: The news bypassed the emperor entirely and came to shepherds.

quiz.q: What did the angel declare the child to be?

options.text: A Savior, who is Christ the Lord, born in the city of David.
options.note: Verse 11 gives the three titles together.

options.text: A baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger.
options.note: That was the sign, but the declaration of His identity was Savior, Christ, and Lord.

options.text: A great prophet sent to Israel.
options.note: He is far more than a prophet; He is the Savior and Lord.

options.text: A future king who might one day rule.
options.note: The angel says a Savior has been born today, not merely a future possibility.

quiz.q: What did the heavenly host proclaim?

options.text: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to those on whom His favor rests.
options.note: Verse 14 is the angels' Gloria.

options.text: That great joy had come for all the people.
options.note: The single angel said this in verse 10; the host proclaimed the glory and peace of verse 14.

options.text: That Caesar's reign would soon end.
options.note: The angels praised God and announced peace, not Caesar's downfall.

options.text: That judgment was coming on the earth.
options.note: Their message was peace and glory, not judgment.

quiz.q: How did Mary respond to all that happened?

options.text: She treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
options.note: Verse 19 records her quiet, reflective wonder.

options.text: She rejoiced and praised God with the shepherds.
options.note: There was joy all around, but Mary's distinctive response was treasuring and pondering.

options.text: She was afraid and told no one.
options.note: She pondered inwardly, but not out of fearful silence; the shepherds spread the news.

options.text: She doubted what the shepherds reported.
options.note: She did not doubt; she treasured the things in her heart.

questions: God bent even Caesar's decree to keep His promise about Bethlehem. Where do you need to trust that God is at work through circumstances that seem far beyond your control?
The Savior was laid in a manger, welcomed with no room. What does the humility of His coming reveal about the kind of God we worship?
The good news of great joy came first to shepherds. How does it encourage you that the gospel runs to the lowly and overlooked, and where might you carry it to them?
The shepherds went, saw, and then spread the message. Having met Christ, who in your life is waiting to hear the news you have received?
Mary treasured and pondered these things in her heart. What would it look like for you to slow down and treasure the wonder of Christ's coming rather than rushing past it?

translationNotes.note: The whole empire is rendered in a footnote as the whole land or the whole world; the word describes the inhabited Roman world subject to the census.

The first census to take place while Quirinius was governor is noted with an alternative, This was the census before Quirinius was governor; the dating has long been discussed, but Luke ties the birth to a real, datable event.

Peace to men on whom His favor rests reflects the best-supported text; an older reading is peace, good will toward men. The favored-ones reading presents peace as God's gracious gift to those He favors.
